newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH GDANSK SHIPYARD FACES FINAL COLLAPSE.
newsitem.headline: POLISH GDANSK SHIPYARD FACES FINAL COLLAPSE.

text.p: Poland's bankrupt Gdansk shipyard, where the anti-communist Solidarity movement was born 17 years ago, faced a final collapse on Wednesday after a bank refused to grant it a survival loan.

The shipyard's administrator appeared set to lay off most of 3,800 workers still employed at the yard, which has operated under bankruptcy rules since August last year, when its debts reached 415 million zlotys ($136 million) and banks refused further credit.
"The decision of the bank will probably make it necessary to terminate employment contracts with shipyard workers," PAP news agency quoted the yard's deputy receiver Janusz Sledzinski as saying.

Earlier in the day, the large state-owned bank, Pekao SA, refused to extend a $100 million loan for the construction of five ships for a German shipowner, saying that terms of the prospective contract were unsatisfactory.
"In our opinion the deadlines for the construction of the ships are too optimistic and their budgets unrealistic," Pekao SA president Andrzej Dorosz told a news conference on Wednesday.

He said that under the contract the construction of the five ships would have to be done in eight or nine months, while the shipyard's track record showed it usually took 13 months to finish such jobs.
The receiver had hoped that the loan and the German contract would have kept part of the yard alive while he and the government sought an investor to save the business.

But the decision of Pekao SA, the second bank to turn down the yard's credit application, appeared to bury such hope, with the government ruling out direct subsidies to save the firm and offering only partial credit guarantees.

The government, grouping ex-communists and a peasant party since 1993, puts the blame for the shipyard's misfortune on its previous management, which was supported by the opposition Solidarity trade union.
"Gdansk shipyard is treated as any company in a free market economy," government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska has recenly said.

But Solidarity -- the defunct Soviet bloc's first free trade union, which toppled communism in Poland in 1989 -- says the government has subsidised other state-owned firms and is now denying help because of the yard's opposition links.
Poland faces parliamentary elections around September this year and Solidarity leads an opposition bloc aiming to challenge the ruling ex-communists and peasants.

The unionists say the feel betrayed by the government, saying it had promised that the shipyard's bankruptcy was just a legal procedure for its overhaul and then kept hopes of a recovery alive with prospects of credit.
"It has been a perfidious way of killing us slowly, in instalments," the deputy head of shipyard's Solidarity, Roman Galezewski, told reporters.
